name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations and fact checking concern the detection, documentation, and prevention of references that do not correspond to real published work, and the verification of claims made in AI research papers. This includes hallucinated citations generated by language models, paper mills, and citation manipulation. The scope extends to checking whether a cited source exists, whether it supports the claim attributed to it, and whether the claim itself is accurate. It sits within research integrity because a false citation can mislead readers and inflate perceived evidence.

sections.body: Fabricated citations and fact checking concern the detection, documentation, and prevention of references that do not correspond to real published work, and the verification of claims made in AI research papers. This includes hallucinated citations generated by language models, paper mills, and citation manipulation. The scope extends to checking whether a cited source exists, whether it supports the claim attributed to it, and whether the claim itself is accurate. It sits within research integrity because a false citation can mislead readers and inflate perceived evidence.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on bibliographic databases, digital object identifier registries, and full-text archives that allow a checker to confirm whether a reference resolves to a real article. It also uses language models and retrieval systems to compare a claim against the abstract or full text of the cited paper. Many fact-checking pipelines rely on scholarly APIs and local document stores, but the core infrastructure is the set of publisher indexes and open repositories that provide ground truth for existence and content.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common method is to parse the reference list of a paper, extract each citation, and query a database such as Crossref or PubMed to see if the title, authors, journal, volume, and page range match a real record. For claim verification, the checker retrieves the cited source and uses a model or human reader to judge whether the source actually states what the citing paper says it states. Some systems also flag statistical anomalies, such as a citation appearing in many papers but never resolving to a real document. The work is often a mix of automated screening and human review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights and risk issues are attribution, defamation, and the integrity of the scholarly record. A false citation can wrongly associate a real author with a paper they did not write, or invent an author who does not exist. Fact-checking outputs must be handled carefully because labeling a paper as containing fabricated citations can affect a researcher's reputation and career. Provenance matters: any correction or retraction should link to the original paper and the verified database record, not to a secondary search tool, so that readers can trace the evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward automated, continuous fact-checking that runs on preprint servers and journal submissions before publication. Language models will likely be used to generate candidate citation checks at scale, while human editors and integrity officers handle appeals and edge cases. There is also growing interest in watermarking or registering citations at the point of generation, so that a reference carries a verifiable provenance trail from the start. Over time, fact-checking may become a standard layer in research infrastructure rather than a post-publication cleanup task.
